h1: Are electric all-in-one brewing systems worth the money?
title: Electric All-in-One Systems: Worth It? | Craft Beer School
desc: An honest look at electric all-in-one brewing systems for Indian homebrewers: what they do well, power and plug needs and when a bag and pot is enough.
teaser: They look like the obvious upgrade. Whether one is worth it depends on how often you brew and what your kitchen wiring can take.
standfirst: Electric all-in-one systems promise temperature control, repeatable brews and less mess. For some homebrewers they are the best money they spend. For others, a pot, a bag and a thermometer still do the job. Here is how to tell which you are.
sections: What an all-in-one system actually is

An all-in-one system is a single insulated vessel with a heating element, a temperature controller and usually a small pump. The grain sits in a perforated basket inside. You mash, lift the basket, sparge over it and boil in the same vessel. Many come with a counterflow or immersion chiller.

In principle it is brew in a bag with the guesswork removed. The controller holds your mash temperature. The pump recirculates wort through the grain bed so the temperature stays even and the wort runs clearer. Some units run a stepped mash programme on their own.
What you get for the money

• Temperature control. Holding 66 °C for an hour on a gas stove means constant fiddling. An all-in-one holds it within a degree or so, which makes mash results repeatable.
  • Step mashing. A rice lager or a wheat beer that benefits from more than one rest becomes simple.
  • A cleaner kitchen. One vessel, no flame, fewer pots.
  • Repeatability. Same grain, same water, same programme, very similar wort. That is the real gain if you want to tune a recipe over several batches.

What you do not get is better beer by default. Fermentation temperature, yeast health and hygiene matter more to the result than the mash vessel does. A well run bag and pot brew beats a badly fermented brew from an expensive machine every time.

This is the part people skip. Typical 20 to 35 litre units run elements of around 2 to 3.5 kW on 230 volts. At 2.5 kW that is a current of about 11 amps, more than a standard 6 amp socket is designed for. You need a proper 16 amp socket on a circuit sized for it, ideally with an earth leakage breaker. Running one from a 6 amp socket through an adapter is how plugs melt.

Talk to an electrician before you buy, not after. Check that the circuit is not shared with the geyser or an air conditioner. Ask about power cuts too. A unit that loses power mid mash will not always resume on its own, so a long cut can spoil a brew.

Then there is the boil. Some smaller units struggle to hold a strong rolling boil at full volume, especially with the lid off. A weak boil leaves more DMS, a cooked sweetcorn flavour, in pale beers. Look for honest user reports of boil vigour at the batch size you plan to brew.
When a bag and pot is enough

If you brew a few times a year, mostly ales, while you are still learning, the money is better spent on fermentation control and good ingredients. A large stockpot, a strong bag, a reliable digital thermometer and a cool box or fridge for fermenting will improve your beer more. Our guides to brew in a bag and to a starter kit in India cover that setup.

An all-in-one starts to make sense when you brew every two or three weeks, want to repeat recipes closely, or are working towards brewing as a job and want to practise controlled, stepped mashing.

Most units are imported, so price, warranty and spare parts are the real questions. Ask the seller who repairs the controller or replaces an element in your city. Ask how long parts take to arrive. Check that the plug and voltage are rated for Indian supply. Budget for a chiller if one is not included. Budget for a stable stand too. A full 30 litre unit weighs more than 30 kg and should not sit on a wobbly kitchen counter.

Second hand units come up in homebrew groups. Check the element, the pump and the controller display. Run a test boil with water before money changes hands.

The kit is never what limits a beginner. Understanding is. Knowing why you mash at 66 °C rather than 70 °C, how to correct a low gravity or what a stalled fermentation is telling you will improve your beer on any equipment. Buy the machine when your brewing has outgrown the pot, not as a way to skip learning.
faqs: Can an all-in-one system make lager?
It handles the mash and boil for a lager well. Lager fermentation still needs a separate way to hold the beer at around 8 to 13 °C, such as a fridge with a temperature controller.
Most homebrewers choose a unit that makes about 20 to 23 litres of finished beer. Smaller units suit apartments but can be harder to fill with high gravity recipes.
Do I need a special socket in India?
Usually yes. Most units draw more current than a 6 amp socket is designed for, so you need a 16 amp socket on a suitable circuit. Ask a qualified electrician first.
Is an all-in-one better than brew in a bag?
It is more consistent and easier to control, but the beer is not automatically better. Fermentation control and hygiene make a bigger difference to quality.
